item.title: UK budget: Growth forecasts cut as Healey unveils £15 billion fiscal buffer
item.description:
The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) lowered its near-term growth forecasts but the government still expects to meet its fiscal rules, with £15 billion of headroom at the end of the forecast period.

The headline growth revisions:

  • 2026 GDP: 1.2% vs 1.1% in March

  • 2027 GDP: 1.0% vs 1.6% in March

  • 2028 GDP: 1.6% vs 1.6% in March

  • 2029 GDP: 1.8% vs 1.5% in March

  • 2030 GDP: 1.7% vs 1.5% in March

  • 2031 GDP: 1.6%

The sharp downgrade to 2027 is the standout number, with growth now expected at just 1.0%. The revisions further out are more constructive but that's the usual tactic.

On the fiscal side, the numbers show a deterioration in the debt outlook:

  • 2026/27 public sector net financial liabilities: 83.2% of GDP vs 82.6% previously

  • 2027/28: 83.8% vs 82.9%

  • 2028/29: 83.8% vs 82.9%

  • 2029/30: 83.1% vs 82.2%

  • 2030/31: 82.3% vs 81.1%

  • 2031/32: 81.7%

The OBR also forecasts a budget deficit of 4.2% of GDP this year, narrowing to 3.4% next year. Public sector net borrowing is projected at 1.8% of GDP in 2030/31, compared with 1.6% in the March forecast.

Healey said the government will spend an additional £14 billion on debt interest this year, underscoring the damage from higher global borrowing costs.

The chancellor ruled out broad-based tax increases and deep cuts to public services, while pledging to maintain the government's fiscal rules. Some of the remaining fiscal headroom will be used to absorb the impact of the Iran war.

The £15 billion buffer is substantially below the £23.6 billion projected in March, but is broadly in line with the £15 billion expected in a Reuters poll of economists.

The market reaction has been relatively calm so far, with the UK 10-year gilt yield extending its decline to 5.34%, down 1.4 basis points on the day.

The bigger picture is that Healey has managed to preserve some fiscal breathing room despite a much more challenging environment. However, £15 billion isn't a particularly large cushion for an economy facing weak growth, elevated debt-servicing costs and considerable geopolitical uncertainty.

The bond market is likely to take some comfort from the commitment to fiscal discipline, but the downgrade to 2027 growth is a reminder that Britain has little room for economic disappointment.

For sterling, the budget looks broadly neutral for now. There is no obvious fiscal shock to drive a selloff, but there is also little here to materially improve the UK's growth outlook. It was last down 16 pips to 1.3284 on the day and little changed since the budget headlines.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US Wholesale inventories 0.6% vs 0.5% estimate
item.description:
• Wholesale inventories: +0.6% MoM. Prior +0.5%, unrevised.

  • Retail inventories: +0.3% MoM. Prior revised to +0.3% from +0.2%.

  • Wholesale inventories: $1,011.5 billion, up 7.4% YoY.

  • Retail inventories: $885.3 billion, up 4.8% YoY.

US wholesale inventories rose 0.6% in September, following a 0.5% increase in August, according to the Census Bureau’s advance estimates.

Retail inventories increased 0.3%, matching August’s upwardly revised gain. Both wholesale and retail inventories remained above year-earlier levels. The figures are adjusted for seasonal variations and trading day differences, but not for price changes.

Quick analysis: Wholesale stockbuilding picked up, while retail inventory growth held steady. Inventories can support gross domestic product (GDP) growth when the pace of accumulation accelerates, but rising stocks can reflect either preparation for stronger sales or unsold goods. Sales data and inflation-adjusted quarterly figures are needed to judge the impact. On their own, these readings offer limited direction for Federal Reserve policy, Treasury yields or the dollar.

What this report measures: Advance inventory estimates track the value of goods held by wholesalers and retailers at month-end. These preliminary figures are subject to revision and are not adjusted for inflation. Traders monitor inventories for clues about demand, business activity and their contribution to GDP.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US September advance goods trade balance -134.9 billion vs -130.2 billion expected
item.description:
• Prior was -132.6

These are the two worst back-to-back months since just before Liberation Day, when goods were flooding into the US to try to front-run Trump's tariffs. Excluding Jan-Mar 2025, it's the worst two-month period ever. Needless to say, tariffs aren't working.

For background, the advance goods trade balance is part of the Census Bureau’s Advance Economic Indicators report, released at 8:30 am ET roughly four weeks after the reference month ends. The same release includes advance estimates for wholesale and retail inventories, making it one of the more useful early inputs for tracking GDP.

The headline figure is the US deficit in goods trade, the difference between the value of goods exported and imported. It’s broken down by end-use category: foods, feeds and beverages; industrial supplies and materials; capital goods; automotive vehicles and parts; consumer goods; and other goods. The figures are seasonally adjusted and in nominal dollars, on a Census basis.

The advance report covers goods only. Services trade, where the US runs a surplus, is added in the full international trade report from the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Economic Analysis, published about a week later. That full report also includes country-level detail and revisions to the advance goods figures.

The data matter mainly for GDP. Net exports are a component of growth, and a wider goods deficit generally subtracts from GDP while a narrower one adds to it. Combined with the inventory figures in the same release, the report often prompts economists and tracking models such as the Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow to revise their estimates.

Trade flows have become far more volatile in recent years. Companies have rushed imports in ahead of tariffs and then pulled back, creating sharp swings in the deficit and in quarterly GDP. Large movements in nonmonetary gold, recorded under industrial supplies, have added further distortions that economists often strip out to judge the underlying trend.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Microsoft and Alphabet report tonight. Wall Street's earnings recovery has a catch.
item.description:
Microsoft and Alphabet report tonight. Wall Street's earnings recovery has a catch.

Earnings reactions are improving across more companies, but some heavyweight stocks are still dragging down the broader picture. Now a Federal Reserve decision, followed by earnings from two AI giants, will put that improvement to the test.

Wednesday, October 28, 2026, could be one of the most consequential days of this earnings season.

Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) report after the market closes, following the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision and press conference. The options market is pricing moves of approximately 5.1% for Microsoft and 6% for Alphabet through Friday.

But before those results arrive, there is something interesting happening beneath the surface of earnings season.

More companies are receiving positive reactions from investors. Yet the largest stocks have not consistently participated in that improvement.

That distinction deserves attention, particularly for anyone holding the S&P 500, Nasdaq-100 or technology-heavy portfolios.

Earnings season is improving, but not quite how you might expect

Earlier this earnings season, Netflix, Tesla and Meta provided reasons for caution.

Their stock reactions were disappointing, with Tesla and Meta offering particularly interesting examples of initial enthusiasm that subsequently faded.

Was Wall Street becoming harder to impress, even when companies delivered respectable results?

The latest earnings-reaction data suggests a more nuanced answer.

Consider these observations from a third-party sample of companies reporting earnings between October 22 and October 27:

Source: Third-party earnings-reaction snapshots reviewed through October 27. Figures relate to sampled earnings-reporting companies, not the performance of the S&P 500 or Nasdaq. Coverage and measurement completeness vary.

October 26 is especially revealing.

More than 71% of companies with usable reactions rose, with an average equal-weight gain of 2.16%.

That sounds like a rather healthy earnings environment.

Yet the market-capitalization-weighted reaction was negative 2.82%.

Verizon, whose reported reaction was approximately -3.49%, exerted a disproportionate influence on that relatively small group.

In other words, many companies were doing well, but the largest companies carried enough weight to overwhelm those gains.

This is an important distinction for investors.

An equal-weight calculation gives every company the same influence regardless of size. A capitalization-weighted calculation gives larger companies greater influence.

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 are capitalization-weighted indices. Consequently, a handful of very large technology companies can substantially influence index performance even when many smaller constituents are advancing.

A healthy majority of stocks does not necessarily mean a healthy capitalization-weighted market.

October 27 delivered a somewhat more encouraging development.

Of 114 companies with usable reactions, 64 advanced. The equal-weight result was positive 1.79%, while capitalization-weighted performance also turned modestly positive, at 0.34%.

There were also 10 upside moves beyond their expected ranges, compared with three downside breaches.

That is constructive evidence, although the sample had important omissions, including Boeing and HSBC, and should not be treated as a complete reading of the earnings season.

The emerging picture is therefore neutral to mildly defensive, but showing tentative signs of improvement.

Some companies are still being rewarded handsomely

It would be a mistake to interpret this earnings environment as uniformly bearish.

Consider three positive reactions from the latest sample:

  • SoFi (SOFI): +13.42%. A substantial repricing that demonstrates investors remain willing to reward individual companies aggressively.

  • Cadence Design Systems (CDNS): +6.49%. A notable positive reaction from a company involved in semiconductor and electronic design software.

  • UPS (UPS): +5.75%. A positive response worth monitoring for clues about investor expectations around logistics and business activity.

These are observations from the supplied earnings-reaction snapshots, not forecasts of continued gains.

The distinction is useful because a cautious overall earnings market can still produce attractive opportunities in individual stocks.

And for traders, the second market reaction can be just as important as the first.

A stock may jump immediately after earnings, only to surrender those gains during subsequent regular trading. Conversely, an initially disappointing reaction can recover as investors reassess the numbers and management commentary.

That is why an earnings beat, an initial price jump and a sustained positive market response should be treated as three different things.

The early October 28 reactions reinforce this need for patience. Initial weakness was observed in Visa, Robinhood, Seagate and NXP Semiconductors, while PPG Industries stood out positively.

Those moves were provisional before the regular session and should not be confused with completed trading-day results.

Microsoft and Alphabet face the next big test

The options market provides a useful indication of how much movement traders are preparing for, although it does not tell us which direction a stock will take.

Indicative pre-earnings estimates using options expiring Friday, October 30, 2026. They are not guaranteed trading ranges or directional forecasts.

There is an additional complication tonight: these implied ranges encompass both the Federal Reserve decision and the earnings announcements.

That means the observed stock moves cannot automatically be attributed entirely to the earnings reports.

For Microsoft, investors will be examining Azure cloud growth, enterprise AI demand, operating margins and the relationship between capital expenditure and future revenue.

For Alphabet, attention will turn toward Google Search, advertising, Google Cloud, AI-related competition and the financial returns on its substantial infrastructure investments.

The issue is not simply whether these companies are growing.

Are they growing strongly enough to justify what investors have already priced into their shares?

The answer may be particularly consequential because spending on AI infrastructure is increasingly being evaluated alongside the revenue and profitability it is expected to generate.

Amazon reports on Thursday, October 29, adding another major test of cloud demand, AI expenditure and profitability.

Together, these reports should help reveal whether investors are becoming more receptive to the financial performance of their largest technology holdings.

Don't hold your breath for a clear answer from the Fed

Before either company reports, markets must navigate the Federal Reserve.

The FOMC statement is scheduled for 2:00 p.m. Eastern, followed by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference at 2:30 p.m.

The broad expectation is for rates to remain unchanged in the 3.75%-4.00% target range.

For those hoping Warsh will provide strong hints about the next policy decision, I would not necessarily hold my breath.

With the US midterm elections approaching on November 3, it would not be surprising if the relatively new Fed Chair chose to communicate cautiously rather than risk unsettling markets.

That is one possible interpretation, not evidence that election timing is determining monetary policy. Elevated inflation and uncertainty about its persistence already provide substantial reasons for caution.

A lack of explicit forward guidance should not automatically be interpreted as dovish or bullish.

Traders may find the more useful information in how Treasury yields, the dollar and equity indices react to the statement and press conference.

For technology stocks, the connection matters.

Higher interest rates and bond yields can reduce the present value of expected future earnings, putting additional pressure on valuations that already depend on substantial long-term growth.

The Fed may therefore change the market's valuation environment before Microsoft and Alphabet release a single earnings number.

Three things worth watching after tonight's announcements

First, watch which companies are participating in the earnings recovery.

Improving breadth is encouraging, but a sustained recovery among the largest companies would provide stronger support for capitalization-weighted indices.

Second, pay attention to the reaction relative to expectations.

A positive earnings surprise does not necessarily translate into a positive stock reaction. Guidance, valuation and investors' expectations for future profitability can matter more than the headline earnings figure.

The approximately 5.1% and 6% implied ranges also give traders a reference for whether price movement is unusually large relative to what options had priced.

Third, don't judge the entire result from the first few minutes of after-hours trading.

Watch whether the initial reaction holds, strengthens or reverses during Thursday's regular session.

A positive reaction that survives the following session would be more persuasive evidence of sustained demand than a short-lived after-hours spike.

Equally, a negative reaction followed by a convincing recovery could indicate that investors are more willing to absorb disappointing news than they were earlier in the earnings season.

Neither outcome alone establishes a durable trend, but both provide useful evidence.

There is more happening beyond Big Tech

Two developments elsewhere in the market are worth connecting to this earnings discussion.

The first is energy.

As investingLive reported, crude oil has been responding to hopes of progress in US-Iran negotiations, although setbacks could revive upward pressure on prices.

There have also been reports of Qatari mediators presenting Iran with a draft deal, with Tehran's response expected by the end of the week. However, conflicting statements and the absence of a confirmed agreement warrant caution.

Why does that matter for stock investors?

Because oil prices influence inflation expectations, which in turn can affect interest rate expectations and equity valuations. Even strong corporate earnings may struggle to lift the wider market if renewed energy inflation pushes bond yields higher.

The second development comes from the banking sector.

HSBC shares fell almost 7% despite a 32% jump in reported pre-tax profit, as weaker-than-expected revenue, stalled wealth income and the absence of upgraded guidance disappointed investors.

It is another reminder that the market evaluates financial results against expectations, rather than simply rewarding companies for reporting higher profits.

The bigger question for investors

Tonight's Microsoft and Alphabet reports are important for more than their individual shareholders.

They offer a significant test of whether the recent improvement in earnings breadth can translate into a more supportive environment for the very large companies that dominate major US stock indices.

The recent evidence is not decisively bearish. In fact, parts of it are becoming more encouraging.

But neither is it sufficiently strong to declare the cautious earnings environment over.

For investors and traders, the next useful signal may not be whether Microsoft and Alphabet beat estimates. It may be whether Wall Street is finally prepared to reward the results, and keep rewarding them after the initial excitement fades.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morning Kickstart: Dollar mixed ahead of Fed, BoC and Big Tech earnings
item.description:
he U.S. dollar is mixed heading into a North American session with two central-bank decisions and major technology earnings on the calendar. The Bank of Canada announces its decision this morning, followed by the Federal Reserve this afternoon. After the closing bell, Microsoft and Alphabet will provide the next important test for technology shares and the AI investment story.

Treasury yields are higher, with the U.S. 10-year yield above 5%. Stock futures are mixed: the Dow is lower, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 point to modest gains. Oil is higher, while gold and silver are trading lower.

Overnight, the biggest currency move came from New Zealand. The RBNZ unexpectedly held its official cash rate at 2.75%, with the committee divided in a 4–3 vote. Governor Anna Breman subsequently indicated that additional increases remain likely, but the decision disappointed markets positioned for an immediate hike. Meanwhile, stronger Australian underlying inflation and hawkish comments from RBA Governor Michele Bullock reinforced expectations for further tightening. Those contrasting developments helped lift the Australian dollar and pressure the kiwi. See investingLive’s Asia-Pacific market wrap.

The Australian dollar leads; the New Zealand dollar lags

The Australian dollar is the strongest of the major currencies in the morning snapshot, while the New Zealand dollar is the weakest. From the U.S. dollar’s perspective, the greenback is higher against the kiwi, sterling and Swiss franc, but lower against the Australian dollar, Canadian dollar, euro and Japanese yen.

NZDUSD is down 1.27% at 0.5608, making it the clear outlier. By comparison, AUDUSD is up 0.14% at 0.7034, while USDCAD is down approximately 0.10% at 1.4034. EURUSD is up 0.07% at 1.1130, and USDJPY is down 0.03% at 157.89. GBPUSD is lower by 0.12% at 1.3287, while USDCHF is up 0.04% at 0.8293.

The broader dollar picture is therefore mixed. The sharp kiwi decline reflects a specific policy surprise, while the moves elsewhere remain relatively modest ahead of the North American events.

Currency ranges remain contained outside NZDUSD

The session highs and lows and the supplied average ranges:

  • EURUSD: 1.1114 to 1.1132 — 18 pips, approximately 28% of its 65-pip average.

  • USDJPY: 157.66 to 158.04 — 38 pips, approximately 45% of its 84-pip average.

  • GBPUSD: 1.3273 to 1.3312 — 39 pips, approximately 55% of its 71-pip average.

  • USDCHF: 0.8284 to 0.8313 — 29 pips, approximately 57% of its 51-pip average.

  • USDCAD: 1.4034 to 1.4068 — 34 pips, approximately 54% of its 63-pip average.

  • AUDUSD: 0.7024 to 0.7054 — 30 pips, approximately 65% of its 46-pip average.

  • NZDUSD: 0.5585 to 0.5689 — 104 pips, approximately 231% of its 45-pip average.

EURUSD has the most room to roam relative to its normal daily activity. USDJPY is also relatively confined, having completed less than half its average range. That leaves scope for an extension if the central-bank news produces a sustained technical break.

NZDUSD has already exceeded twice its average range. That does not rule out additional movement, but traders should recognize that a substantial repricing has already occurred. Average ranges provide context; they do not establish a ceiling or guarantee that a quieter pair must move farther.

U.S. stock futures are mixed

  • Dow industrial average futures: down 105 points.

  • S&P 500 futures: up 9.5 points.

  • Nasdaq 100 futures: up 103 points.

The opening indications show a modestly firmer tone in the S&P and Nasdaq, although the Dow is lagging. The important question is whether those gains hold and broaden once regular trading begins, with the Fed announcement and earnings still ahead.

Treasury yields move higher

The 2-year Treasury yield is 4.7577%, up 2.07 basis points, while the 5-year yield is 4.8675%, up 2.55 basis points. The 10-year yield is 5.0155%, up 2.25 basis points, and the 30-year yield is 5.3125%, up 0.75 basis point.

The larger increases are in the shorter and intermediate maturities. I will be watching whether those gains extend or reverse after the Fed. A dollar break accompanied by a sustained move in yields would provide more evidence of a broader repricing in policy expectations.

European yields are also higher. Germany’s 10-year yield is 3.365%, France’s is 4.953%, and the UK’s is 5.354%. Italy’s 10-year yield is up 3 basis points at 4.532%.

European stocks are mostly lower

  • Germany’s DAX: up 0.04%.

  • France’s CAC 40: down 0.12%.

  • UK’s FTSE 100: down 0.25%.

  • Spain’s IBEX 35: down approximately 1.37%.

  • Italy’s FTSE MIB: down 0.01%.

Spain is the weakest of the supplied European benchmarks, while the German and Italian indices are little changed.

Oil rises; gold and silver retreat

U.S. crude oil is trading at $101.69, up $1.48, or 1.48%. Gold is lower by approximately $14.54 at $4,045.79, while silver is down 1.22% at $53.7421. Bitcoin is modestly higher at $81,097, up $286, or 0.35%.

Firmer oil keeps energy prices in focus ahead of the Fed’s inflation assessment. Gold is trading lower alongside higher Treasury yields, although the mixed dollar performance suggests caution in attributing its move to a single factor.

FOMC preview: A hold is expected, but the message matters

In his FOMC preview, “A hawkish hold as markets watch for signals about timing and extent of further tightening,” investingLive’s Giuseppe Dellamotta outlines a base case of unchanged rates at 3.75%–4.00%. His October 27 preview cited approximately 90% market pricing for a hold and an 80% probability of a December hike.

With no new economic projections or dot plot expected, attention shifts to the statement and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference. The key issue is how strongly the Fed reinforces the need for additional tightening. A more forceful inflation message could pressure risk assets, while a more neutral tone could allow a relief rally.

For traders, an expected decision can still produce an unexpected reaction. The market responds to the difference between the message delivered and the message already priced in. I will be watching whether an initial break can hold beyond a key technical level. A failed break would tell a different story from a move that establishes acceptance above resistance or below support.

Bank of Canada and the North American calendar

The Bank of Canada provides the first major policy catalyst, with its rate announcement and Monetary Policy Report due at 9:45 a.m. ET. Governor Tiff Macklem and Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers follow with a press conference at 10:30 a.m. ET. The updated outlook and guidance will be important for USDCAD before attention shifts to the Fed.

The main scheduled events, in chronological order, are:

  • 8:30 a.m. ET: U.S. advance goods trade balance, advance wholesale inventories and retail inventories excluding autos.

  • 9:45 a.m. ET: Bank of Canada rate decision and Monetary Policy Report.

  • 10:30 a.m. ET: Bank of Canada press conference.

  • 2:00 p.m. ET: Federal Reserve policy decision.

  • 2:30 p.m. ET: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference.

The trade and inventory figures provide information on the contributions to economic growth, but the two central-bank decisions are the main scheduled policy events.

After the close: Microsoft and Alphabet headline earnings

The session’s event risk continues after the closing bell, with Microsoft and Alphabet the main earnings reports to watch. As Adam Button discusses in “Earnings macro week ahead: The Fed and Big Tech report on the same day,” their spending plans have implications beyond individual share prices. AI investment is an important part of the broader economic picture, making guidance on future spending especially relevant. Chipotle also reports after the close, providing another perspective on consumer demand.

For Microsoft, I will be watching Azure growth, AI-related revenue and the capital-spending outlook. The question is whether growth and profitability provide sufficient support for the investment being made. A headline earnings beat may not settle that question if guidance raises concerns about costs or the timing of returns.

For Alphabet, the focus includes Google Cloud, search advertising, AI monetization and spending plans. Advertising provides a useful read on business demand, while cloud performance helps assess whether the AI investment cycle continues to generate revenue growth.

Chipotle offers a different economic signal. Customer traffic, comparable sales and management’s pricing commentary should help distinguish changes in underlying demand from growth driven by higher menu prices.

The practical takeaway is that the afternoon reaction to the Fed may face another test after the close. Policy expectations will drive the first assessment; company results and guidance will then provide fresh evidence on demand, investment and profitability.

In the morning video above, I take a look at the three major currency pairs—EURUSD, USDJPY and GBPUSD—from a technical perspective. For each pair, I outline the bias, the risk-defining levels and the targets that would give either the buyers or sellers more control.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive European session wrap: Stocks tread cautiously as Fed decision and big tech earnings loom
item.description:
Headlines:

  • Crude oil remains under pressure amid US-Iran deal hopes; setbacks could push prices to new highs
  • Qatari mediators presented Iran with new draft deal; Iran's response expected by the end of the week
  • Gold rebounds on renewed hopes for US-Iran deal as focus shifts to FOMC decision
  • Wall Street faces a double test as Fed decision and Microsoft, Alphabet earnings loom
  • Heads up: UK autumn budget puts Healey to the test as gilt markets await fiscal reassurance
  • Germany consumer sentiment remains weak ahead of November as inflation fears cloud recovery outlook
  • Germany's trade struggles with China set to put Asia-Pacific deficit on course for record high

Markets:

  • AUD leads, NZD lags on the day
  • 10-year Treasury yields up 2.5 bps to 5.017%
  • Gold down 0.3% to $4,045
  • WTI crude oil up 1.9% to $101.78
  • European equities little changed; S&P 500 futures +0.1%

It was a steadier session after the hustle and bustle in Asia trading, as markets are taking a bit of a breather awaiting the bigger events to come this week.

Earlier in the day, we saw hotter-than-expected Australia inflation data and the RBNZ surprising with a decision to hold the overnight cash rate at 2.75% in a narrow 4-3 vote. But after the big moves then, there wasn't much follow up in European morning trade as traders are preparing for the Fed decision and big tech earnings later in the day.

The dollar was much steadier on the session, with EUR/USD up just 0.1% to 1.1130 and keeping within an 18 pips range. Meanwhile, USD/JPY is flat at 157.90 on the day.

Oil prices continue to hold firmer after reports of a Houthi attack on a major Saudi refinery, as well as the US warning that there might be a brief escalation to the war with Iran after the midterm elections. WTI crude is up nearly 2% to $101.78.

Besides that, broader risk sentiment was much calmer even as 10-year Treasury yields nudged a little higher to above 5% again. European stocks are more tepid with lights changes seen across the board while US futures are holding just a touch higher as tech shares look to build on the gains from yesterday. Big tech earnings will be in focus today though with Meta and Alphabet both set to report earnings, but only after the closing bell.

Elsewhere, gold is also looking more tentative as traders continue to sit on edge with price just above the $4,000 mark. The precious metal is down slightly today to $4,045 but all eyes will be on what happens with the bond market after the Fed decision as well as the broader risk mood to see if gold has appetite to chase a downside break below the figure level.

Coming up, we will have the UK autumn budget announcement shortly and that will be a focus for the pound and gilts. And after that, traders will have the BOC decision to weigh up first before we get to the Fed decision later in the day and then big tech earnings to round things off.

There's still plenty to play for, so don't expect this calmer mood in markets to persist as the key risk events above are likely to inject volatility into trading conditions - not to mention alongside month-end flows in the coming days.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: EUR/USD nears key 1.1067 swing level ahead of Fed and ECB decisions. What's next?
item.description:
USD:

The Federal Reserve is widely expected to keep interest rates unchanged. With no new projections or dot plot expected at this meeting, changes in Fed Chair Warsh's or statement's language will be the main focus.

Despite higher September inflation data strengthening the case for further tightening, key Fed members have signalled little urgency to deliver a back-to-back rate hike in October. A hawkish hold remains the base case as the debate centres around the timing and extent of further tightening rather than direction.

Warsh is expected to reiterate that monetary policy is not sufficiently restrictive and that additional tightening is warranted. He's also seen reaffirming the commitment to price stability but cautioning against overreacting to individual data points.

Markets are already pricing an 80% chance of a rate hike in December, so the focus will be more on the 2027 outlook. Traders see roughly two more rate hikes next year, with the first fully priced in move in April.

A surprise rate hike would trigger strong risk-off flows. The US dollar and Treasury yields might initially react positively to the decision, but I think the reaction will be quickly faded as growth concerns should intensify amid falling stock markets.

A largely neutral outcome that avoids signalling an imminent rate hike could be taken as dovish and trigger a correction in the US dollar. I would also expect the same reaction but with less magnitude in case the Fed just delivers on the hawkish hold expectations, avoiding major surprises.

EUR:

On the EUR side, the ECB is widely expected to keep rates unchanged, while maintaining its data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting approach. Inflation accelerated to 3.8% in September, driven by energy prices, while core inflation showed more limited increases.

Rising energy costs and the risk of second-round inflation effects remain hawkish risks but increased growth concerns and tighter credit conditions argue for caution. Markets will focus on any signals about further tightening, with the December rate hike probability standing around 68%.

France is likely to dominate the press conference, with traders looking for clues on whether widening sovereign spreads and fiscal uncertainty could prompt a more dovish ECB stance or potential intervention through the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI). A hawkish surprise is unlikely in the current context.

The next key catalyst for the euro should be the vote on France’s 2027 state budget which is scheduled for November 3. This vote concerns the revenue section of the budget. The full budget vote is scheduled for November 17.

The vote matters as a test of the government's ability to deliver fiscal consolidation. A smooth passage would offer some relief and could give the euro a boost, while a rejection or major concessions that weaken the deficit-reduction plan could put further pressure on French bonds and the euro.

EURUSD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that EURUSDis approaching a key swing level around 1.1067. If the price gets there, we can expect the buyers to step in, with a defined risk below the level, to position for a correction into the downward trendline around the 1.15 handle. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break lower to increase the bearish bets into the 1.08 level next.

EURUSD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we have a downward trendline defining the bearish momentum. If we get a pullback, we can expect the sellers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep pushing into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to increase the bullish bets into new highs.

EURUSD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, there’s not much we can add here as the sellers will have a better risk to reward setup around the trendline, while the buyers will look for the price to come into the key swing level or a break above the trendline. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

Today we have the FOMC rate decision. Tomorrow, have the ECB rate decision and we get the US GDP report, the US PCE and the latest US Jobless Claims figures. On Friday, we conclude the week with the Eurozone GDP and the US Employment Cost Index.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Zcash extends gains as geopolitical fears ease ahead of the FOMC decision. What's next?
item.description:
Zcash extended the gains yesterday as renewed hopes for a US–Iran deal helped improve risk sentiment across crypto markets. item.title: Heads up: UK autumn budget puts Healey to the test as gilt markets await fiscal reassurance
item.description:
UK chancellor Healey has a rather unenviable task at hand today. He is expected to deliver a budget that keeps households happy, businesses afloat, and bond investors calm. All while trying to convince everyone that the government isn't running short of money. Well, good luck with that.

It is definitely quite the juggling act for his first autumn budget. And with borrowing costs still elevated and fiscal headroom shrinking, there's not exactly much room for him to get creative.

So, what goodies can Healey realistically pull out of the bag today? And perhaps more importantly for markets, it is the question of who's going to end up paying for them?

Here are some of the key measures to watch out for:

  • Bank tax hike: A potential reversal of the bank surcharge cut from 8% to 3%, which could raise over £2 billion annually
  • Online marketplace taxes: Requiring platforms like Amazon and eBay to collect VAT from more UK sellers, potentially raising £1 billion to fund business rates relief for smaller shops
  • Energy bill relief: Over £1 billion in support for poorer households, including a possible £100 increase to the existing £150 Warm Home Discount
  • Fuel duty freeze: Another extension looks likely, although that could cost the Treasury up to £2.7 billion annually
  • Housing support: A proposed 20% equity loan for first-time buyers purchasing new-build homes, requiring deposits of just 2.5%

Now, that is quite the shopping list for someone with limited fiscal room to work with.

The government's already strained fiscal position isn't helping with the situation, with its fiscal headroom potentially being halved from £24 billion to around £12 billion amid rising borrowing costs. So, that just means gilt traders will have plenty to scrutinise today.

Besides that, the OBR forecasts and borrowing projections could arguably matter more than the spending headlines. A more credible fiscal plan could offer some relief to gilt yields, particularly at the long-end of the curve. However, any suggestion of unfunded spending will only risk another bond market tantrum and that won't be a pleasant sight.

As we look to the budget announcement later (expected at 1230 GMT), do keep a watchful eye on how the energy relief measures might influence inflation expectations and in turn BOE rate hike pricing.

For Healey himself, I reckon a boring budget might actually be a win for his political standing. But whether or not markets agree is a whole other matter.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Macro pulse: Has the RBNZ shock exposed a bigger problem with central bank rate pricing?
item.description:
The central bank bonanza definitely kicked off with a bang today. While markets have been talking about the Fed all week, the RBNZ offered traders a bit of a reality check earlier today to not take anything for granted. Even with traders pricing in a roughly 90% chance of a 25 bps rate hike, the central bank instead held rates at 2.75% in a close 4-3 vote.

The surprise in terms of market reaction is captured by the kiwi, with NZD/USD down 1.3% to 0.5605 today. But is there a broader lesson that goes beyond what we have seen so far?

For the better part of the last decade, traders have grown accustomed to central banks offering plenty of forward guidance and holding their hands through major policy decisions. Central bankers would more or less signal their next move well in advance, giving traders a relatively clear path to follow in the lead up to the upcoming meeting.

Now, that kind of luxury appears to be slowly disappearing.

The fact of the matter is that central banks are having to deal with a very difficult balancing act at the moment. Inflation pressures remain stubborn and higher borrowing costs as well as mounting fiscal pressures are taking a toll on growth conditions, making it tough for central banks to commit to a particular policy path.

In looking at the RBNZ today, policymakers weren't convinced that another rate hike was necessary just yet even with inflation running at 3.7% and projected to rise to 4.4% in the final quarter of the year. That's a damning assessment of the current landscape that major central banks are dealing with.

While inflation remains the core problem that needs to be addressed, the risks to growth and the need to assess earlier tightening moves were enough to tip the balance towards waiting in the case of the RBNZ.

So, does that mean we should expect similar surprises from the likes of the Fed or ECB this week?

Well, not necessarily I would say. All else being equal, I would not overreact to one decision from a major central bank. After all, the RBNZ has had a knack for a few surprises every now and again.

For the Fed, they are widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged today. Meanwhile, the ECB is very much expected to stay on the sidelines tomorrow. Those remain fairly reasonable base case scenarios for the respective central banks.

In my view, the RBNZ surprise is less about predicting the next central bank shock and more about how markets should approach policy expectations from here.

Now, the Fed has to weigh persistent inflation against the risk of tighter financial conditions. As for the ECB, they must also contend with rising borrowing costs and fiscal concerns across Europe.

While the decisions this week are likely to play out according to market expectations, what happens after that is still up for interpretation. As it stands, no central banks want to commit to a rate hike today only to discover that growth conditions have deteriorated sharply a few weeks later.

Come what may, the Fed and ECB are two big names that typically do not try to upset markets and cause unnecessary volatility - especially at a time like this when borrowing costs are surging and inflation risks are mounting. If there's an issue with the market pricing relative to their communique, policymakers would usually voice that out in the weeks running up to the next meeting. But then again, never say never when it comes to markets. That is a lesson every trader will learn at some point.

For the time being, we should still expect the next run out in the central bank bonanza to stick to the script even after the RBNZ surprise. However, whether or not policymakers will validate or invalidate pricing for upcoming decisions in the months ahead will be a separate issue.

But in seeing how things play out with the RBNZ, it is best to be reminded of the fact that a 90% probability is still at the end of the day just a market expectation. It is not a promise from policymakers to take action.

And in a time when central banks are progressively favouring flexibility over firm commitments, traders may have to get comfortable with a little more uncertainty when positioning for the months ahead.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Germany's trade struggles with China set to put Asia-Pacific deficit on course for record high
item.description:
For quite some time now, Germany's export struggles are hardly anything new. A lot of that comes down to push to diversify away from China in recent times but Beijing's own ambitions to become more self-sufficient haven't exactly helped matters either.

That has slowly exerted a toll on Europe's largest economy, especially when you consider how much Germany's industrial sector has relied on Chinese demand over the years.

And a new report from Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI) today is offering another warning of the challenges to come, with the report projecting that Germany is set to post a record trade deficit of nearly €146 billion with Asia-Pacific in 2026.

The detailed projection shows that exports to the region are expected to decline by 3.2% to €185.3 billion. Meanwhile, imports are forecast to rise by 6.4% to €330.9 billion. But perhaps the most telling detail is that excluding China, Germany's trade deficit with Asia-Pacific would narrow to just under €35 billion. Yowza.

Just by that alone, you can see where the biggest problem lies for Germany.

For years, German manufacturers have enjoyed a strong position in China - especially when it came to automobiles and machinery. However, those days look to be over as Chinese manufacturers have stepped up to close the gap, and in some areas, even move ahead of their German counterparts.

There's no better example to that than the auto industry. German carmakers were once among the biggest beneficiaries of China's growing middle class but now, domestic brands are now taking a much bigger slice of the market especially as the growing majority are leaning towards electric vehicles.

According to the report, German auto exports to China fell by more than 30% in the first seven months of 2026. That's quite the drop. Meanwhile, machinery exports declined by 18% over the same period.

That is clear evidence of the reality that China is becoming less dependent on German industrial products. And if that isn't bad enough for Germany, the issue now is that they are still heavily reliant on Chinese imports for electronics, machinery and other industrial components.

And with EU-US trade tensions adding another layer of uncertainty, that's hardly an encouraging backdrop for Germany's export-driven economy.

The only small bright spot is that the likes of India and Southeast Asia are becoming more important trading partners. However, trying to replace the scale of their dealings with China isn't something that can happen overnight.

I would argue that the bigger issue for Germany now is not just that they are facing another difficult year for exports. It is more so the fact that the competitive landscape has changed considerably over the years and they are being left behind. Europe's largest economy has to face the reality that the traditional industrial strengths it has relied on for so long may no longer provide the same advantages they once did.

And that is a tough pill to swallow, and an even tougher one to think about how they can fix that growing problem.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

In any case, the data here won't do much to change anything for the ECB decision tomorrow. And in looking to December, it just reaffirms the backdrop that the German economy is still showing uneven signs in terms of growth recovery as households and consumption remain a bit of an issue.

What does the data measure?The GfK consumer climate index measures German households' confidence in their financial prospects and willingness to spend. It draws on consumer surveys covering income expectations, purchasing intentions and saving behaviour.

Why does it matter to markets?Household consumption is an important driver of German economic activity. Weak confidence suggests consumers may delay major purchases and prioritise savings, limiting domestic demand and making a sustained economic recovery more difficult.

How does this fit the broader economic picture?Germany's economic outlook remains uneven. Recent business surveys suggest some improvement in expectations but households are still struggling with purchasing power concerns and economic uncertainty. The contrast between business optimism and consumer pessimism suggests that any recovery may struggle to gain traction without stronger household spending.

item.description:
Even with the latest developments out of Australia earlier today, AUD/USD is finding it tough to make any meaningful push higher. The pair continues to trade around 0.7030 on the day, once again knocking on the door of key technical resistance near its 100-day and 200-day moving averages.

The latest Australia CPI report was hotter than expected, with trimmed mean inflation rising to 3.7% against expectations of 3.6%. That certainly doesn't make the RBA's job any easier, especially with oil prices adding to inflation pressures.

And RBA governor Bullock didn't exactly mince her words either, warning that inflation remains "far too high". Her comments pretty much reinforces the narrative that the central bank is almost certainly poised for another rate hike next week, giving the aussie a fundamental reason to hold firmer. Or at least that is the case in theory.

But looking at the AUD/USD chart, buyers still have some convincing to do.

The double-bottom pattern near 0.6900 has set the pair up for a decent rebound in the past week or so, with the latest run up testing key resistance around 0.7030-50. And that is where the 100-day (red line) and 200-day (blue line) moving averages are starting to converge around. That makes for a rather stubborn technical hurdle, with buyers repeatedly struggling to establish a firm break above the region since last week.

A sustained push above the 200-day moving average at 0.7054 would be a more encouraging development, potentially opening the door towards 0.7100 before the descending trendline resistance closer to 0.7220 comes into focus next.

On the downside, the 0.7000 level remains the first key support to watch, followed by the 0.6900-0.6920 region and then the rising trendline support near 0.6900 as well.

So, what's next for the pair this week?

Well, the Fed could be one to have the bigger say in what happens next. A more hawkish message from Warsh & co. could give the dollar another lift, making it more difficult for AUD/USD to chase a break higher.

And with broader risk sentiment still looking fragile, particularly around tech stocks, the aussie might not exactly get much help from that side of the equation either. It all will depend on how big tech earnings play out later in the day, with watchful eyes on Microsoft and Alphabet earnings after the closing bell. That will also in turn have some potential spillover impact on how the bond market reacts.

In other words, there's still a lot to play for in broader markets for the second half of the week.

So even if the domestic story may be turning more supportive for the aussie, I wouldn't be convinced that AUD/USD can sustain the next leg higher until buyers can clear the resistance zone highlighted above.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.description:

Having said that, the price momentum continues to side with sellers for now as the drop this week puts a test of the 14 October low at 1.1111 in focus. The swing low there will be a more important level to watch, with EUR/USD looking to stick with a further downside push ahead of the main events this week.

Then, there is one for USD/JPY at the 158.00 level, with the strike holding within 30 pips of the spot level. That could help keep price action anchored around the figure ahead of the cut, particularly if markets settle into a holding pattern ahead of the Fed today. And lastly, there is one for AUD/USD at the 0.7005 level. The expiries could offer some attraction if price action drifts lower ahead of the cut, although the technicals appear to be having more of a say for now.

So, that region will offer a key resistance layer for AUD/USD buyers to get through this week. And they will likely have to weigh the hotter-than-expected Australia inflation data against the Fed and broader risk sentiment before firming up any conviction to push through.

As for the downside, the key hourly moving averages at 0.7005-23 will be the notable near-term downside layer holding up the pair. item.title: Wall Street faces a double test as Fed decision and Microsoft, Alphabet earnings loom
item.description:
Wall Street enjoyed a bit of a breather in overnight trading, as the S&P 500 gained by 0.6% and Nasdaq closed higher by 1.2%. It's a welcome relief after drop in the past two weeks as tech shares bounced back, but there are still plenty of reasons for investors to be nervous in trading this week.

For one, the rebound overnight was not all too convincing once we start to dig a little deeper beneath the surface. It was largely driven by big tech names with most of the stocks in the S&P 500 actually closing lower. That's not a good signal on market breadth now, is it?

And with the Fed decision coming up later today, followed by earnings from Microsoft and Alphabet after the closing bell, there's still quite a lot that could go wrong.

Now, the Fed is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged. So, I don't see the decision itself being much of a surprise. All eyes will be on Fed chair Warsh's press conference as markets will be listening closely for any signals on December, particularly with Treasury yields still hovering near 5%.

With that in mind, any suggestion that policymakers are becoming even more uncomfortable with the inflation outlook could easily put another dent in risk sentiment.

And that will be especially relevant for tech stocks, where higher borrowing costs and lofty valuations are already making investors question just how much optimism is justified.

Microsoft's earnings will be closely scrutinised for whether its AI growth can continue to justify the enormous spending commitments. In particular, there will be plenty of watchful eyes on its Azure growth, cloud margins and capital expenditure especially.

As for Alphabet, they will face similar scrutiny with Google Cloud performance, AI monetisation and infrastructure spending all under the microscope.

At this point, I'm not sure that investors will be satisfied in just hearing that AI demand remains strong. It seems that they might want clearer evidence that all those billions being spent are translating into sustainable earnings growth. And that's where the real test for the AI trade lies at the moment.

It's going to be quite a tricky test for stocks and broader markets in the coming day(s). While a more hawkish Fed could put renewed upward pressure on Treasury yields, disappointing earnings guidance could reignite concerns over the AI spending boom. The latter is one that could even see both yields and stocks fall at the same time.

So while the calmer mood overnight is a little encouraging, it is best to be mindful that the real test for markets this week is still yet to come.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: European markets brace for Fed decision as hot Australia CPI, RBNZ surprise and oil rally stir nerves
item.description:
It has been quite an eventful start to the day so far as the central bank bonanza rolls into town. That is putting inflation back in the spotlight with there already being plenty to digest before European traders get to their desks and before we even get to the main events later today.

To start with, we saw Australia's latest CPI report came in hotter than expected with trimmed mean inflation rising to 3.7%. That's not a good look and RBA governor Bullock was quick to respond in warning that inflation remains "far too high". The numbers certainly strengthen the argument for another rate hike, with Bullock's response underscoring the narrative that the central bank is facing an increasingly uncomfortable inflation outlook.

As such, that is now seeing markets step up their pricing for the next RBA meeting on 3 November, with traders pricing in roughly 76% odds of a 25 bps rate hike.

Meanwhile, the RBNZ delivered arguably the bigger surprise of the session after keeping its official cash rate unchanged at 2.75% in a narrow 4-3 vote. Markets had been expecting a 25 bps rate hike today, so the decision has definitely caught traders off guard and sent the kiwi sharply lower. NZD/USD is down 1.1% to 0.5615 on the day currently.

Having said that, the central bank hasn't abandoned its tightening bias altogether as the minority continued to take on a more hawkish stance. But at least for now, the shock of the decision is the one that will be reverberating as the RBNZ conviction doesn't look as strong as markets had thought coming into today.

Apart from central banks, oil prices are also back on the move following a reported Houthi attack on a major Saudi refinery. Adding to that, the US has also reportedly warned of a possible short but intense military campaign against Iran after the midterm elections. So, that is pushing oil prices higher with WTI crude nudging back above $101 on the day.

That's a lot to take in already and put together, they're not helping with the inflation narrative - especially when the bond market continues to be rather nervous this week, despite the recent pullback in yields.

10-year Treasury yields are still holding around 5.01%, so that is keeping borrowing costs and equity valuations firmly in focus. And higher oil prices will only serve to complicate that picture further, potentially making it harder for central banks to bring inflation under control.

As we head towards European morning trade, do keep a close watch on Treasury yields and the broader risk sentiment. However, the day ahead will be all about the main events tom come later in US trading mostly.

The Fed decision is the obvious headline event but big tech earnings from Microsoft and Alphabet will be just as important in shaping the market mood. With yields still elevated and investors questioning the returns on massive AI spending, big tech names don't have too much room in disappointing markets.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Topix explained: why Japan’s biggest-ever index overhaul will cull 683 stocks by 2028
item.description:
The immediate effect comes at Thursday’s close, when around $60 billion of passive trades is expected to cause sharp, short-lived price swings and heavy volume in affected stocks. That can briefly distort the Topix and individual names, which is why hedge funds have been positioning in advance. Over time, the quarterly weight cuts create steady selling pressure on smaller, less liquid companies and support larger stocks such as Kioxia. That may widen the gap between Japanese large caps and small caps. The 2027 re-evaluation gives companies a reason to improve liquidity and free float, which could encourage more unwinding of cross-shareholdings and buybacks. That fits the governance push foreign investors have rewarded. Watch for a temporary gap between the Topix and the Nikkei 225, which isn’t affected.

--- Japan is turning its sprawling Topix into a leaner, more investable benchmark, and with about ¥166 trillion tracking it, the reshuffle starts with a $60 billion trade on Thursday and keeps going for two years.

Summary:

  • The Topix’s largest-ever overhaul takes effect on October 30, with about $60 billion of passive trading expected at Thursday’s close, the Japan Times reported.
  • 683 companies that failed new liquidity and free-float tests will be phased out, with their weights cut in eight quarterly steps from January 2027 to zero in October 2028.
  • Companies that meet the criteria at an October 2027 re-evaluation stop being cut and remain in the index.
  • The index is projected to shrink from 1,669 members after October to about 986 by mid-2028.
  • About ¥166 trillion of passive assets track the Topix, per Daiwa, so index funds must sell dropped stocks and buy additions.
  • Kioxia’s weighting is set to rise, with hopes of around $13 billion of inflows, Bloomberg reported.

Japan’s main equity benchmark is undergoing the biggest overhaul in its history this week, with changes to the Topix index taking effect from Friday, October 30. Around $60 billion of passive trading is expected at Thursday’s close as index funds reposition, according to the Japan Times, and the reshuffle will continue to shape flows into Japanese stocks for the next two years.

The Topix, short for Tokyo Stock Price Index, has long been one of the broadest major equity benchmarks, covering a large share of companies listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange. That breadth has drawn criticism, because it includes many small, thinly traded companies that are hard for large investors to buy. The Japan Exchange Group has been reforming the index to make it more investable, cutting the number of constituents from around 2,200 to around 1,700 in a first phase that ended in January 2025.

The second phase is far more ambitious. Under the periodic review published on October 7, stocks are now judged on annual trading value and on the market value of shares freely available to investors. Some 683 companies that failed to meet those tests will be phased out, while dozens of others have been added. Exchange data show the index had 1,636 members at the end of August and 1,669 after October’s changes, but the count is projected to fall to 986 once the transition is complete in mid-2028, plus any companies that requalify.

The phase-out is gradual by design. Rather than removing the 683 stocks at once, the exchange will cut their index weight in eight quarterly steps of 12.5 percentage points, starting in January 2027 and reaching zero in October 2028. Companies that meet the criteria at a re-evaluation in October 2027 will stop being cut and remain in the index. From October 2028, the Topix will be rebalanced annually.

The stakes are large because so much money tracks the index. Daiwa Securities estimates around ¥166 trillion of passive assets follow the Topix, including index funds and exchange-traded funds. When a stock’s weight is cut, those funds must sell it, and when a stock is added or up-weighted, they must buy, regardless of valuation. That mechanical demand is why hedge funds have been positioning ahead of the changes, the Japan Times reported, aiming to profit from price moves in affected stocks around the rebalancing.

Some well-known names stand to benefit. Memory chipmaker Kioxia is set to see its weighting rise, with hopes of around $13 billion of inflows, Bloomberg reported earlier this month. For the companies being phased out, the gradual schedule gives them time to lift trading liquidity or free float, through measures such as unwinding cross-shareholdings, in order to requalify.

Analysts see the reform as part of Tokyo’s wider push to improve corporate governance and valuations. Some argue that concentrating the benchmark in larger, more liquid companies could lift the market’s overall valuation and reinforce the long-running tilt toward large caps, while smaller companies dropped from the index could face weaker demand from passive investors.

For investors, the immediate focus is Thursday’s close, when the first rebalancing trades are expected. The longer-term effect will play out every quarter until 2028, making the overhaul a slow-moving but persistent force on Japanese equity flows.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

Summary:

  • RBA Governor Bullock said inflation is far too high and likely to exceed the August forecasts. Q3 trimmed mean CPI rose to 3.7% y/y, above forecasts, strengthening the case for a November 3 hike.
  • The RBNZ held the OCR at 2.75% in a 4-3 vote, surprising markets, but Governor Breman later said further hikes are likely at coming meetings.
  • The NZ dollar fell sharply and the Australian dollar rose, sending AUD/NZD strongly higher.
  • Oil rose, with Brent around $115, on a Houthi claim of a strike on Saudi Arabia’s biggest refinery and a WSJ report that the US warned Gulf states of a possible post-midterms campaign against Iran.
  • Israeli exit polls pointed to no clear election result.
  • The Kospi surged 6% after SK Hynix posted a roughly sevenfold jump in Q3 operating profit and unveiled about $75 billion in shareholder returns. The Nikkei rose 1.4%.
  • US Treasury Secretary Bessent said crypto rules can advance through agency action despite the Senate’s failure to pass the Clarity Act.

Australia: Bullock and CPI build the case for a November hike Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock struck a hawkish tone at Senate Estimates, saying inflation is likely to run above the RBA’s August forecasts as the re-escalating Middle East conflict lifts energy prices and the labour market looks a little tighter than previously judged. After the data, she said inflation is far too high, that it is difficult to completely look through supply shocks and that domestic demand still exceeds supply, though she declined to give guidance on next week’s decision.

The September quarter CPI backed her concerns. The trimmed mean, the RBA’s main gauge of underlying inflation, rose 1.0% in the quarter and 3.7% year on year, above the 3.6% expected, while monthly headline inflation climbed to 4.3% in September. Together, the data and Bullock’s comments strengthen the case for a rate hike when the Board concludes its meeting on November 3.

New Zealand: a surprise hold, then hawkish guidance The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held its official cash rate at 2.75% in a 4-3 vote, defying around 90% market pricing for a hike and forecasts from all five major local banks. The majority, including Governor Anna Breman, cited lower-than-expected headline inflation of 3.7%, smaller pass-through from fuel and subdued wages, though all members agreed tighter policy is likely to be needed. At her press conference, Breman said further rate increases are likely at coming meetings and could extend into restrictive territory, and that a persistently weak New Zealand dollar could add to imported inflation.

FX: AUD/NZD jumps on policy divergence The New Zealand dollar fell sharply after the RBNZ decision, while the Australian dollar gained on the hotter CPI and Bullock’s comments. The diverging signals from the two central banks drove a strong rise in AUD/NZD.

Oil and geopolitics: supply risks return Oil prices rose, with Brent around $115 a barrel, after Yemen’s Houthis said they had struck Saudi Arabia’s largest refinery, a claim Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm. Geopolitical risk was reinforced by a Wall Street Journal report that the US has told several Gulf Arab states to prepare for a possible short, intense military campaign against Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, with President Donald Trump leaning toward a large strike but yet to decide. Market chatter also centred on the possibility of renewed Israeli strikes on Iran, although Israel’s defence minister has said there was no intention to attack before the election. Exit polls from Tuesday’s Israeli election pointed to no clear result, with official results due on November 4.

Equities: Kospi soars as SK Hynix delivers Asia-Pacific stocks followed Wall Street higher, where the Nasdaq outperformed. South Korea led the region, with the Kospi surging 6% and the Kosdaq up 3%, after SK Hynix reported a roughly sevenfold jump in third-quarter operating profit to around 83 trillion won, ahead of forecasts, as memory chip prices surged on AI demand. The chipmaker unveiled shareholder returns of about 100 trillion won, around $75 billion, for 2026, including more than 60 trillion won of share buybacks and cancellations and more than 30 trillion won in dividends, alongside a quarterly dividend of 20,000 won per share. Net profit missed forecasts, and the company said it expects DRAM demand to grow by a mid-20% rate in 2027. Elsewhere, Japan’s Nikkei rose 1.4%, China’s Shanghai Composite gained 0.5% and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng added 0.2%.

Crypto policy: Bessent eyes agency route US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington can still deliver crypto regulation without new legislation. Speaking at Ripple’s Swell conference, he described the Senate’s failure to pass the Clarity Act as disappointing, but said Treasury would use its convening power to advance a regulatory framework through agency action with the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
